query: For high-entropy alloys intended for extreme environments, what single testable intervention hypothesis could improve elevated-temperature mechanical properties? State the intervention without limiting its class, the proposed mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, the temperature and application boundaries under which it should hold, the prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment whose outcome would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a trace amount of boron to a refractory high-entropy alloy will lead to the in situ formation of fine boride precipitates along the grain boundaries, thereby enhancing grain-boundary cohesion and significantly improving elevated‐temperature yield strength and ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: An equimolar or near-equimolar refractory high-entropy alloy (e.g., HfMoNbTaTiZr) without any trace dopants at the grain boundaries.
generation.intervention: Introduce a trace doping (around 0.1 at.%) of boron during alloy synthesis.
generation.conditions: Mechanical testing at elevated temperatures in the 1200°C to 1600°C range, typical for aerospace or nuclear reactor applications.
generation.structural_mediator: Precipitation of fine hexagonal boride phases (likely (Hf, Zr)B2) at the grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Boron addition promotes grain-boundary precipitation of borides, which enhances intergranular cohesion. This microstructural change mitigates grain-boundary sliding and brittleness at high temperatures, leading to improved work hardenability, ductility, and yield strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline alloy without boron, the boron-doped alloy is predicted to exhibit a higher yield strength and better ductility at temperatures between 1200°C and 1600°C.
generation.baseline: The same refractory high-entropy alloy composition prepared without any boron doping.
generation.boundary: This effect is expected to hold for refractory high-entropy alloys designed for extreme high-temperature applications (such as aerospace turbine engines and nuclear reactor components), especially within the temperature range where grain-boundary integrity is critical (approximately 1200°C to 1600°C).
generation.uncertainty: While prior evidence indicates improved grain-boundary cohesion from trace boron additions, the exact magnitude of mechanical property enhancement at the targeted elevated temperatures remains to be precisely quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of the refractory high-entropy alloy: one identical set without boron and one with 0.1 at.% boron doping. Subject both sets to homogenization treatment and then perform mechanical tests (e.g., compression/tensile tests) at elevated temperatures (1200°C to 1600°C). Microstructural analysis via electron microscopy should be used to confirm the presence and distribution of boride precipitates in the doped alloy.
measurements: Microstructural characterization of grain boundaries (presence/absence of boride precipitates)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the boron-doped alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in yield strength and ductility at the targeted high temperatures compared to the undoped alloy, or if the microstructural analysis fails to reveal the formation of boride precipitates at the grain boundaries, then the hypothesis is falsified.

## Abstract
AbstractTo develop strong refractory high-entropy alloys for use at elevated temperatures as well as to overcome grain-boundary brittleness, an equimolar HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy was prepared, and a minor amount of boron (0.1 at.%) was added into the alloy. The microstructures of the alloys were characterized, and their macro-to-microscale mechanical properties were measured. The microstructural observations indicated that the matrices of both the alloys were composed of a body-centered cubic solid-solution structure, and the added boron induced the precipitation of hexagonal close-packed borides (most likely the (Hf, Zr)B2) at the grain boundaries. The modulus and hardness of differently oriented grains were about equivalent, suggesting a diminished anisotropy, and many small slips occurred on multiple {110} planes. While the hardness of the matrix was not increased, the intergranular precipitation of the borides markedly raised the hardness of the grain boundaries. Owing to the enhanced grain boundary cohesion, the work hardenability and ductility were effectively improved with the addition of boron.Keywords: refractory alloy, high-entropy alloy, boride, grain boundary, mec

After the first development of RHEAs in 2010, over 150 kinds of compositions have been reported, with their potential for use in high-temperature applications such as gas turbine engines and rocket nozzles. Various studies focused on ductility enhancement [,], better oxidation resistance [], and nuclear reactor material applications [,]. According to a review by Senkov et al. [], the only alloys to pass high-temperature compression tests at 1600°C were MoNbTaW and MoNbTaVW. The main reason for the difficulty to perform compression tests at extremely high temperatures is the lack of suitable material as a jig material that provides high strength at extremely high temperatures. Recently, Wang et al. strengthened the grain boundary of an MoNbTaW-refractory high-entropy alloy through doping with B or C in trace amount, which simultaneously increases room-temperature strength and toughness []. This study provides a good strategy to increase the ductility of RHEAs by doping suitable elements.
